problem: R2R VLN agents built as encoder-decoder models overfit instructions from seen environments: GloVe or from-scratch word embeddings carry no context, and only 69% of bigrams are shared between training and evaluation. The decoder is trained with either teacher-forcing, which causes exposure bias, or student-forcing, whose random rollouts drift off the path so the instruction no longer applies.
motivation: ImageNet pretraining transfers well in vision, but language-only transfer learning had not been shown for VLN instruction understanding. With the panoramic action space, trajectories are short (up to about 7 steps). At that length teacher-forcing is usually preferred, yet its exposure bias leaves the agent unable to recover from its own mistakes, which matters most in unseen environments.
key_idea: Encode instructions with a large pretrained language model (BERT or GPT, fine-tuned in two stages) and train the action decoder with stochastic sampling, a per-step Bernoulli coin flip between teacher and sampled actions, to get a simple agent that generalizes to unseen environments.
insight: Both ingredients help generalization independently and add up. In the ablation (Table 3, val-unseen SR/SPL), the LSTM encoder goes from TF 42/39 and SF 40/31 to SS 53/48, and BERT goes from TF 51/47 and SF 51/42 to SS 59/55. Student-forcing looks best on val-seen (BERT SF SR 73) but overfits, with long unseen trajectories (TL ~13 m) and low unseen SPL, so a fixed mix of teacher and sampled actions is the better bias-variance point. Language-only pretraining narrows the seen/unseen gap: with SS, BERT reaches 55 unseen SPL vs 48 for LSTM, and BERT generalizes better than GPT (51). Aggregating all three instructions by mean-pooling grounded contexts is also a large factor: PreSS goes from 43/38 (single instruction) to 56/50 (all three) on val-unseen without data augmentation.
method: Pretrained-LM instruction encoder: BERT-base or GPT produces contextualized word embeddings e; an LSTM turns them into textual features h^e_l, and a soft attention from the decoder state h_t gives the textual context c_t = Σ α_l h^e_l.

Two-stage learning: (i) embedding stage with the LM frozen, training only the LSTM encoder and decoder (lr 1e-4); (ii) fine-tuning stage that trains all parameters including BERT at a smaller lr (5e-5), because naive full fine-tuning overfits quickly.

Multi-instruction aggregation: when several instructions describe one trajectory, the per-instruction grounded contexts c_{i,t} are mean-pooled into z_t = (1/M) Σ c_{i,t}, producing a single trajectory (setting M).

Action decoder: a single-layer LSTM (h=1024) following the Speaker-Follower follower design. It uses one-hop attention over panoramic ResNet view features conditioned on h_{t-1}, and the state update is h_t = LSTM([s_t, a_{t-1}], h_{t-1}) in the panoramic action space.

Stochastic Sampling (SS): at each training step the action is a = δ a^T + (1-δ) a^S with δ ~ Bernoulli(ε), mixing teacher and policy-sampled actions for state transitions. Unlike scheduled sampling, ε is a fixed constant rather than decayed; its value is not reported.
Training: MLE with Adamax; batch size 24 for pretraining and 16 for fine-tuning.

numbers_note: The paper does not state which evaluation setting the main Table 2 / Table 3 numbers use. They match Table 3 (BERT-base SS) and exceed Table 1 setting M without data augmentation (56/50 unseen), which suggests the multi-instruction setting M plus data augmentation; a commented-out appendix caption says 'with Data Augmentation'. The GPT SS val-unseen NE 3.05 is copied as printed, although it looks inconsistent with SR 56. Stochastic-sampling ε is not reported.
results: PreSS reaches 57 SR / 53 SPL on R2R test-unseen and 59 SR / 55 SPL on val-unseen with greedy decoding. It beats the previous best EnvDrop (51/47 test, 52/48 val-unseen) by 6 SPL points and also beats search-based methods such as FAST and Regretful on SPL. Against the Speaker-Follower follower baseline without augmentation, PreSS improves val-unseen SPL by +13 (single instruction) and +24 (three instructions).
limitations: The main numbers appear to aggregate all three instructions per trajectory (setting M), an advantage single-instruction baselines do not have; in the single-instruction setting PreSS gets only 43 SR / 38 SPL on val-unseen and is worse than seq2seq on val-seen.
Evaluated only on R2R with precomputed ResNet features and the discrete nav-graph; there is no continuous or real-robot evaluation.
Full fine-tuning of BERT overfits quickly and needs a two-stage schedule; the SS ratio ε is fixed and not reported or analyzed.
